steps.premise: Drawing from the path can mean balancing a sketchbook on one's knee.
steps.action: Set a book at a place with seating and a clear view of a plant worth sketching.
steps.consequence: The visitor can draw the plant from a comfortable position.
steps.quote: Station a book where a seated visitor can see an interesting plant clearly, so drawing needn't involve balancing the book on one knee in a path.

steps.premise: Putting an imperfect mark in a public book can feel daunting.
steps.action: Invite a gardener to leave an unfinished pencil sketch near the beginning.
steps.consequence: Seeing tentative marks makes it easier to make one's own.
steps.quote: Let a gardener contribute an unfinished pencil study near the front. A few searching lines make putting an imperfect mark in a public book feel easier.

steps.premise: Some visitors have no more than a minute to draw.
steps.action: Suggest a subject as small as a single leaf edge.
steps.consequence: They have a drawing they can complete in the time available.
steps.quote: Offer a prompt as small as drawing the edge of one leaf, giving visitors with only a minute a subject they can finish.

steps.premise: Looking at a whole planted border can make choosing what fits on the page difficult.
steps.action: Provide a small cardboard frame to look through.
steps.consequence: The visitor can pick out a manageable group of stems to draw.
steps.quote: A small cardboard viewfinder helps someone faced with a whole border pick a patch of stems that fits on the page.

steps.premise: A person drawing while guiding a child's hand already has both hands occupied.
steps.action: Use a binding that stays open on its own.
steps.consequence: The adult can hold the pencil and help the child at the same time.
steps.quote: Choose a binding that lies open by itself so a visitor can hold a pencil in one hand and steady a child's hand with the other.

steps.premise: Strong marks on one face of a sheet could make the reverse harder to use.
steps.action: Give visitors soft graphite for shared sketchbooks.
steps.consequence: They can make bold drawings and still leave usable space on the other side.
steps.quote: Supply soft graphite for the communal books so a bold drawing on one side of a sheet leaves the next side usable.

steps.premise: Some visitors struggle to hold a narrow pencil.
steps.action: Offer pencil grips in a range of widths.
steps.consequence: They can select a grip that feels comfortable to draw with.
steps.quote: Set out a few pencil grips of different widths to give visitors who find a slim barrel awkward a comfortable way to draw.

steps.premise: A visitor might be unable to read the garden's written welcome.
steps.action: Show a picture of a hand drawing in an open book.
steps.consequence: They can recognize that they too are invited to draw.
steps.quote: A simple picture of an open book and a drawing hand can invite someone to join in even if they can't read the garden's welcome sign.

steps.premise: Later readers may want to know when the plants in a sketch looked that way.
steps.action: Invite artists to add a date at their discretion.
steps.consequence: In autumn a reader can look back and see when the magnolia was already in bloom.
steps.quote: Encourage artists to jot down the date if they wish. People leafing back in autumn can then spot how early the magnolia opened.

steps.premise: A drawing can make someone curious about the actual plant.
steps.action: Include space beside a sketch for the plant's location in the garden.
steps.consequence: A reader can find that seed head or other feature and see it up close.
steps.quote: Leave space for the plant's garden location beside a drawing, helping another visitor track down an intriguing seed head for a closer look.

steps.premise: People browsing can occupy the volume others are waiting to draw in.
steps.action: Place a copy of a finished book nearby for people to look through.
steps.consequence: The current volume is available to those wanting to make a sketch.
steps.quote: Set up a second copy of a completed book for browsing nearby, freeing the current volume for visitors who are waiting to draw.

steps.premise: A sudden rain shower could spoil a season's drawings.
steps.action: Give the book a sheltered, dry spot and make its return location clear.
steps.consequence: Visitors can put it back where the drawings are protected from rain.
steps.quote: Give the sketchbook a dry home under cover with a clear place to return it, so a sudden shower doesn't soak a season's drawings.

steps.premise: Other guests can end up in a reference photo in a busy glasshouse.
steps.action: Ask people to turn the sketchbook toward the plant for the photo.
steps.consequence: They can frame the reference without including other visitors.
steps.quote: Ask visitors to turn the book toward the plant when taking a reference photo, keeping other guests out of the frame in a busy glasshouse.

steps.premise: An outline on the page misses the sounds and smells of the scene.
steps.action: Welcome a short written observation of a sound or scent next to the drawing.
steps.consequence: The page records a sensory detail the drawing alone would lose.
steps.quote: Welcome a line about a scent or sound alongside a sketch, letting the page preserve something its outline alone can't convey.

steps.premise: Some visitors like to test their marks before adding one to a public page.
steps.action: Keep scrap paper with the pencils.
steps.consequence: They can try a stroke privately before drawing in the shared book.
steps.quote: Keep a few pieces of scrap paper in the pencil tray for people who want to try a mark privately before committing it to the shared book.

steps.premise: A child and an adult may see the same flower differently.
steps.action: Let them draw side by side on the same spread if both wish to.
steps.consequence: They can compare the two pictures of their subject.
steps.quote: Let children and adults work side by side on a spread if both want to. Two views of the same flower give them something concrete to compare.

steps.premise: Drawing small plant details up close could otherwise require picking material.
steps.action: Invite people to sketch the fallen pods already on the table.
steps.consequence: Visitors can study details within reach while leaving the plants alone.
steps.quote: An invitation to draw the fallen pods already on the table brings small details within reach without asking visitors to pick anything.

steps.premise: Tiny details call for a fine pencil point.
steps.action: Provide a pencil sharpener at the drawing station.
steps.consequence: Visitors can restore the point for detailed work.
steps.quote: A pencil sharpener with a closed shavings cup lets visitors restore a fine point for tiny details without scattering wood curls into the beds.

steps.premise: Sharpening can leave wood shavings in the garden beds.
steps.action: Use a sharpener with an enclosed cup.
steps.consequence: The cup collects the shavings as visitors sharpen their pencils.
steps.quote: A pencil sharpener with a closed shavings cup lets visitors restore a fine point for tiny details without scattering wood curls into the beds.

steps.premise: A loose page may fall out and take a drawing with it.
steps.action: Have a volunteer check each book at closing and make a small repair when a leaf is loose.
steps.consequence: Drawings can be secured before they go missing.
steps.quote: Ask a volunteer to flip through each volume for loose leaves at closing, when a small repair can still save a drawing from going astray.

steps.premise: A visitor may want to find the sketchbook station again with a friend.
steps.action: Give visitors a take-home garden map slip with the station marked.
steps.consequence: They can use it to find their way back together.
steps.quote: Provide a slip that visitors can take home with the sketchbook station marked on a garden map, making it easier to return with a friend.

steps.premise: Returning visitors may want to compare what people noticed at the same time in earlier years.
steps.action: Shelve completed sketchbooks by season.
steps.consequence: Readers can locate earlier observations from the month they have in mind.
steps.quote: Give finished volumes a shelf sorted by season, so a returning visitor can find what other people noticed during the same month in earlier years.

steps.premise: Some visitors enjoy drawing with other people while observing in silence.
steps.action: Occasionally offer a quiet drawing time before a garden tour.
steps.consequence: They can try the shared books in company under quiet conditions.
steps.quote: Offer an occasional quiet drawing period before a garden tour, letting visitors who like to observe in silence try the books in company.

steps.premise: Signing or introducing oneself publicly may deter a visitor from adding a drawing.
steps.action: Put up a written invitation explicitly welcoming unsigned drawings.
steps.consequence: Someone can contribute a page without having to identify themselves.
steps.quote: Post a written invitation to leave drawings unsigned, so adding a page doesn't require making a public introduction.

steps.premise: A small vein or texture in bark may be too hard to see to draw.
steps.action: Leave a magnifying lens at the sketchbook station.
steps.consequence: Enlarging the detail lets a visitor draw it as the subject itself.
steps.quote: Keep a magnifying lens at the station for visitors curious about a vein or a patch of bark, turning a barely visible feature into a subject of its own.
